article.title: Curbing Cancerous Capitalism
article.author: Peter Laarman
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A recent public webinar presented in tribute to the late great Rev. James M. Lawson, Jr. on his birthday reminded me that this latter-day prophet often invited us to use his term, “plantation capitalism,” to describe how things really work in the U.S. economy. In using this expression, Lawson did not mean to suggest that contemporary wealth creation depends on actual slavery—on human trafficking—although to some degree it clearly does . What he meant is that the economic operating system we inherit, in which mostly white men and white-adjacent men enjoy unlimited freedom to exploit others, is built upon a foundation laid by centuries of chattel slavery: centuries during which the default wage was zero. When actual slavery dominated the national economy, plantation capitalism’s capacity to metastasize was widely feared. During the 1850s, alarmed white farmers and mechanics in the Northeast and Midwest joined forces with the abolitionists to oppose the advance of what they called “ The Slave Power .” They saw slavery’s expansion as coming for them—for white people—by undercutting standards for all work. But “free soil and free labor” also became a rallying cry for white privilege, with catastrophic consequences, preventing the emergence of a multiracial democracy with economic equity in the wake of an incredibly bloody civil war. That epochal failure and white racism’s long infestation of U.S. trade unionism obviously problematize applying a plantation capitalism frame to our understanding of economic power. But I believe problematizing the frame actually makes it more rather than less useful. Related: Recalling the Torments of a Radical Truthteller We can learn from past failure as we confront the planter class in our own era. These days, a steady media drumbeat reminds us that wage gains consistently trail inflation, but that is not nearly the half of it. Working peoples’ share of total national income has been steadily declining for decades, as business elites outsource production to drive down wages and crush unions, with workers forced to replace their union cards with credit cards. Buying their way to political dominance, these same elites shifted the tax burden from their own shoulders to the shoulders of wage workers. They also forced workers to bear the burden of paying for their own pensions, eliminating the defined benefit plans that used to be commonplace. Warehouse and delivery work—a rapidly expanding sector both during and after COVID—is by now very rigidly regimented , with delivery drivers having to pee into milk cartons and soda bottles in order to meet daily quotas. Large-scale agriculture? Just think of conditions at industrial farms and processing plants: the picture there is absolute peonage, with injury and death rates rising through the roof. Work in the growing health care sector? It’s ever more routinized, monitored, and dehumanized, as any doctor or nurse or pharmacist can tell you. Related: Detestable, Damnable Debt – And Who Is Really to Blame And that’s just the employment side. On the consumption side, it’s just as bad if not worse. Private equity has most likely bought up whole subdivisions in the area where you live. It probably owns your mortuary and your veterinarian’s practice. It might own your hospital. It undoubtedly owns your grandmother’s nursing home and her medical device provider. The private equity sharks are always in for the kill. They don’t build anything. They make their money by “restructuring” businesses in order to squeeze out labor costs. Service quality and employment conditions both plummet when this happens. How could it be otherwise? Add to this the AI revolution, a technical innovation that is rightly compared to nuclear fission in its potential for doing grave harm to humanity. In a working democracy, we would put severe controls on when and how this technology is applied. But we do not have a working democracy. We have never had a working democracy. We have rule by a handful of plantation capitalists who exercise the right to do whatever they want whenever they want. Demanding a New Economy While Building a New Culture: These Times Require Both Do not think this horror will end when and if Trumpism begins to subside. All of the recent shifts toward savage inequality have been many decades in the making, enabled by well-fed Democrats as much as by plutocratic Republicans. And they all go back to the default situation in these United States of America: the very wealthiest always call the tune. Curbing this cancer is a challenge for the ages. A relatively easy step is tapping into the deep disenchantment and rage of young workers who have relatively little difficulty relating to the concept of plantation capitalism. Their rage could begin to make itself felt in the coming midterm elections, and we could also see an even wider rebellion against corporate rule in the form of local direct actions, consumer boycotts, and nontraditional labor insurgency. Related: The Furious Defense of a Hollow "Center" And then what? The corporate state has consistently shown itself capable of doling out enough crumbs to tamp down most rising insurgencies. Our overlords are accustomed to assigning this pacification task to the Democrats. If Democrats regain political power in 2026 and 2028, will we settle for minor mitigation around the edges, or will we press on for radical restructuring and do the necessary work to make radical reconstruction a lasting reality? The hardest challenge remains the capacity of white racism and related wealth worship to thwart real restructuring. But dealing with this is not the insuperable barrier that the racial fatalists make it out to be. White racism is resilient, potent, and far from defeated. But W.E.B. Du Bois, who first developed the concept of the “wages of whiteness,” never believed that persistent ruling class manipulation of race created a permanent barrier to building cross-racial solidarity. Which is not to say that limiting racism’s poison doesn’t still stand out as by far the most daunting organizing challenge. Daunting, yes, but not insuperable. Our political imaginaries need to grow more creative. We need to begin again. Ultimately, we need to defeat economism itself. We need to create a whole new culture that isn’t about getting and spending and in which acquisitive individualism will be seen as the pathological behavior it really is. But we also bear moral responsibility for preventing the worst harms of the existing order while seeking to dismantle it altogether. We are called to do both things. This takes us back to James Lawson: he was a true visionary who preached and taught the gospel of spiritual transformation, but he could and did operate on both planes. Even as he called for a spiritual rebirth, he directly assailed the specific spiritual wickedness embodied in oppressive social structures. And in combating these structures he was a supremely gifted organizer. He taught his disciples how to bring critical analysis to bear, assess all possible resources, map a strategy, be prepared to shift tactics as needed, and play the long game. He never underestimated the depth and durability of racism’s poison, but he also believed that cross-racial solidarity was possible. He showed how it can work in the labor empowerment campaigns he helped to inspire and lead in Los Angeles and elsewhere. We can count on the guardians of plantation capitalism to fight to the finish to keep things as they are, using all of their considerable powers to manufacture consent. We know by now what they will do. The only question is what we will do.
